title: Matrix Calculus, PCA and Whitening

intro.x: Machine learning writes its objectives in matrices: $\norm{X\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{y}}^2$, $\log\det\Sigma$, $\tr(W\T AW)$. To optimise them we need derivatives with respect to vectors and matrices. This chapter develops the small set of rules that cover almost every case, derives least squares and the Gaussian maximum likelihood estimate by differentiation, re-derives principal component analysis as a constrained optimisation problem, and introduces whitening and the Kronecker product. The rules are not mysterious: each follows from the one-dimensional rule applied componentwise, and the main difficulty is bookkeeping, which these tools make routine.

blocks.x: For a scalar function $f:\R^n\to\R$ the gradient $\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\in\R^n$ is the vector of partial derivatives $(\nabla f)_i=\partial f/\partial x_i$. It satisfies, to first order,
f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})=f(\mathbf{x})+\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\T\mathbf{h}+o(\norm{\mathbf{h}}).

For a vector function $\mathbf{F}:\R^n\to\R^m$ the Jacobian $J_{\mathbf{F}}\in\R^{m\times n}$ has entries $\partial F_i/\partial x_j$, and $\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})\approx\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x})+J_{\mathbf{F}}\mathbf{h}$. The Hessian of a scalar $f$ is the symmetric matrix $H_{ij}=\partial^2f/\partial x_i\partial x_j$, the Jacobian of $\nabla f$.

The most reliable way to differentiate matrix expressions is the differential method: expand $f(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{h})$ to first order, collect the terms linear in $\mathbf{h}$ and read off the gradient from the form $\nabla f\T\mathbf{h}$. It avoids index gymnastics and catches transposition mistakes.

The chain rule is composition of linear maps (Chapter 9): Jacobians multiply. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation (backpropagation) evaluates the product $J_{\mathbf{G}}\T\nabla\phi$ from the output backwards, which is cheap when the output is a scalar.

blocks.x: For a quadratic $\tfrac12\mathbf{x}\T A\mathbf{x}$ with $A\succ0$, gradient descent with the best step size contracts the error by $\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}$ per step, where $\kappa=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$. If $\kappa=10^4$ the contraction is $0.9998$ and thousands of steps are needed: the level sets are long thin ellipses and the iterates zigzag across the valley. This is the reason for preconditioning, momentum, conjugate gradients (Chapter 21) and normalisation layers.

For samples $\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_N\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\Sigma)$ the log-likelihood is
\ell=-\tfrac N2\log\det\Sigma-\tfrac12\sum_i(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})\T\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu})+\text{const}.

Setting $\nabla_{\boldsymbol\mu}\ell=\Sigma^{-1}\sum(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu)=\mathbf{0}$ gives $\hat{\boldsymbol\mu}=\bar{\mathbf{x}}$. For $\Sigma$, write $P=\Sigma^{-1}$: $\ell=\tfrac N2\log\det P-\tfrac12\tr(PS)$ with $S=\sum(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf{x}_i-\boldsymbol\mu)\T$, using $\mathbf{v}\T P\mathbf{v}=\tr(P\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}\T)$. Then $\nabla_P\ell=\tfrac N2P^{-1}-\tfrac12S=0$ gives $\hat\Sigma=S/N$, the sample covariance.

Let the rows of $X\in\R^{N\times d}$ be centred data points with sample covariance $C=X\T X/N\succeq0$. We want a unit direction $\mathbf{u}$ such that the projections $X\mathbf{u}$ have maximal variance.

The problem $\max_{\norm{\mathbf{u}}=1}\mathbf{u}\T C\mathbf{u}$ is solved by the eigenvector $\mathbf{q}_1$ of $C$ for its largest eigenvalue $\lambda_1$, with optimal value $\lambda_1$. More generally the $k$-dimensional subspace maximising the retained variance $\tr(U\T CU)$ over $U\in\R^{d\times k}$ with $U\T U=I$ is $\Span\{\mathbf{q}_1,\dots,\mathbf{q}_k\}$, and the maximum is $\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_k$.

Via Lagrange multipliers: the Lagrangian $\mathbf{u}\T C\mathbf{u}-\mu(\mathbf{u}\T\mathbf{u}-1)$ has gradient $2C\mathbf{u}-2\mu\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}$, so $\mathbf{u}$ is an eigenvector with $\mu$ its eigenvalue, and the objective equals $\mu$; so the best is the top eigenvector. This is also the Rayleigh–Ritz theorem (Theorem 15.8). For $k$ directions, write $U$ in the eigenbasis: $	r(U\T CU)=\sum_i\lambda_i
orm{\mathbf{q}_i\T U}^2$ where the weights $w_i=

Among all rank-$k$ orthogonal projections $UU\T$, the one minimising the mean squared reconstruction error $\frac1N\sum_i\norm{\mathbf{x}_i-UU\T\mathbf{x}_i}^2$ is the PCA projection, with error $\lambda_{k+1}+\dots+\lambda_d$.

blocks.name: Interview check
blocks.title: two views of PCA, one answer

blocks.x: Maximum variance: directions along which the data spread most. Minimum reconstruction error: the subspace that best preserves the data. They coincide because the total variance is fixed and splits, by Pythagoras, into the part kept and the part lost. The fraction of variance explained by $k$ components is $\sum_{i\le k}\lambda_i/\sum_i\lambda_i$. In practice compute PCA by the SVD of $X$ (Theorem 17.14), not by forming $C$.

PCA is not scale-invariant: a feature measured in millimetres dominates one in metres. Standardise features (unit variance) first unless the scales are meaningful. PCA also captures only second-order (linear) structure, and large variance does not imply relevance to the prediction target: a high-variance direction can be pure noise, while a predictive direction can have small variance.

If $C=Q\Lambda Q\T\succ0$, the matrix $W=\Lambda^{-1/2}Q\T$ satisfies $WCW\T=I$. The transformed data $\mathbf{z}=W\mathbf{x}$ has identity covariance: it is whitened (decorrelated and scaled). Another valid choice is the symmetric $W=C^{-1/2}$ (ZCA whitening). Whitening is Gram–Schmidt of the random variables, with respect to the covariance inner product.

$d_M(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\sqrt{(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})\T C^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})}$ is the Euclidean distance after whitening, since $\norm{W\mathbf{x}-W\mathbf{y}}^2=(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})\T W\T W(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})=(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})\T C^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y})$.
The level sets of the Gaussian density $\propto\exp(-\tfrac12d_M^2)$ are the ellipsoids of Chapter 15 with axes along the eigenvectors of $C$ and lengths proportional to $\sqrt{\lambda_i}$.

For $A\in\R^{m\times n}$ and $B\in\R^{p\times q}$ the Kronecker product $A\otimes B\in\R^{mp\times nq}$ is the block matrix $(a_{ij}B)$. The vectorisation $\mathrm{vec}(X)$ stacks the columns of $X$ into one long vector.

(i) $(A\otimes B)(C\otimes D)=(AC)\otimes(BD)$; (ii) $(A\otimes B)^{-1}=A^{-1}\otimes B^{-1}$ and $(A\otimes B)\T=A\T\otimes B\T$; (iii) $\mathrm{vec}(AXB)=(B\T\otimes A)\mathrm{vec}(X)$; (iv) if $A,B$ have eigenvalues $\lambda_i,\mu_j$, then $A\otimes B$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_i\mu_j$, and $\det(A\otimes B)=\det(A)^p\det(B)^m$ for $A\in\R^{m\times m}$, $B\in\R^{p\times p}$.

Property (iii) turns matrix equations into ordinary linear systems: the Sylvester equation $AX+XB=C$ becomes $(I\otimes A+B\T\otimes I)\mathrm{vec}(X)=\mathrm{vec}(C)$, and the Lyapunov equation $AX+XA\T=Q$ is the special case from stability theory. In machine learning, the Fisher information of a layer is approximated by a Kronecker product (K-FAC), and tensor products underlie multi-head attention in the einsum notation.

For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $A\otimes B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0&2\\1&0&2&0\\0&0&0&1\\0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Its eigenvalues are $\{1,1\}\times\{1,-1\}=\{1,1,-1,-1\}$, matching Theorem 19.11(iv).
